Tolliver Clock and Watch Workshop
Restoring fine mechanical timepieces for collectors and households
Tolliver Clock and Watch Workshop specializes in the repair and restoration of mechanical clocks and watches, from pendulum wall clocks and mantel clocks to hand-wound and automatic wristwatches. We have served the district for more than twenty-five years.
Our benches are dedicated entirely to spring-driven mechanisms, so we do not service battery or quartz movements, and we do not carry out jewelry or eyeglass repair. Restoration of older pieces often requires small parts to be made by hand on site, and every completed repair carries a full twelve-month guarantee covering both parts and labor. How long a repair takes depends on the service it needs, as shown below.
Services and turnaround
Service | Typical turnaround |
Cleaning and oiling | 2 weeks |
Full movement overhaul | 6 weeks |
All items must be brought to the workshop in person, as we cannot accept timepieces sent by mail. We recommend bringing any original winding keys or paperwork, although this is not required. A written estimate is prepared for every item, and work begins only after you approve it. To arrange a repair, please telephone the workshop during opening hours. When you call, please tell us the make and movement type of your timepiece so that we can set aside enough time at the bench.

AROUND THE REGION
Chess Championship to Return This Autumn
Regional association invites players of every level to compete in Riverton
By Colin Ashby, Community Affairs Correspondent
RIVERTON — September 18
The Selby District Chess Association will hold its annual Selby Open Championship at Riverton Civic Hall this autumn, and organizers say they expect one of the strongest turnouts in years. The event is open to players of every skill level, from schoolchildren trying competitive play for the first time to seasoned club members.
For more than a decade the association has served the wider county, and alongside the championship it also runs regular monthly tournaments in the neighboring towns of Hadleigh and Penhurst. "We want this championship to reach every corner of the region, not simply one town," said Malcolm Frost, the association's president. He added that membership has climbed steadily each year and that newcomers are always welcome.
Entries close on October 6, and the championship itself is scheduled for Saturday, October 14. The entry fee is fifteen dollars, which covers all rounds and a light lunch. Interested players may sign up in person at the association's office on weekday afternoons or by telephone during the same hours.
----------------------
Strong Field at Selby Open Championship
Continuing our coverage of the region's amateur competitions
By Teresa Colgan
RIVERTON — December 9
The Selby Open Championship was held at Riverton Civic Hall on Saturday, December 6. The contest drew more than 120 players, the largest field it has ever recorded, and spectators filled the hall throughout the day. Organizers reported that every scheduled round finished on time despite the crowded program.
In the Open division, Carol Sutton captured first place after a tense final round that lasted well past the afternoon. The junior title went to Simon Hale, a newcomer competing in only his second tournament. Chief judge Raymond Delaney praised the overall standard of play, while association president Malcolm Frost thanked the many volunteers who kept the long day running smoothly.
Full standings for every division will be posted at the association's office and on its website by December 20, where players may also find details of next year's calendar.

Community Spotlight
By Frances Doyle
The Larkmead Community Craft Center is looking for a few extra pairs of hands, and it hopes local hobbyists will answer the call.
Leading the effort is Estelle Monroe, who spent more than fifteen years teaching art at a nearby high school before retiring three years ago. Since then she has volunteered at the center every week, and this autumn she takes charge of its expanding beginner workshop program. The classes draw dozens of residents each month, from schoolchildren to retirees, and Monroe says the waiting list keeps growing.
To keep pace, the center needs volunteer assistants who can support newcomers during sessions. Assistants set out materials, answer simple questions, and encourage first-timers who feel unsure. The program is meant to welcome enthusiastic hobbyists rather than trained professionals, and Monroe stresses that a friendly, patient manner matters far more than any formal qualifications. There is one practical condition: because assistants work alongside beginners at the worktable, the center asks that each volunteer already practice at least one craft of their own. Anyone interested can complete a short interest form, available at the front desk or on the center's website.
Have a hobby you love to share? Larkmead wants to hear from you.

Community News
By Gordon Pyle
The Bramford Historical Society will open its new Local History Center to the public next Saturday, offering residents a permanent home for the town's records, photographs, and everyday objects. The center occupies the former Trescott Flour Mill on Bell Lane, a stone building that stood empty for nearly twenty years before volunteers restored it over two summers. The ground floor holds a reading room and a small exhibit gallery, and the upper floor has been fitted out for workshops and document storage.
"A history center is only as rich as the community that fills it," said Ronald Ashworth, the society's director. "I would encourage every household in Bramford to look through their attics and drawers and donate old letters, maps, and family photographs, so that the collection reflects the whole town."
Residents who wish to take part may bring items to the center throughout opening week or ask a volunteer about lending materials for copying. To learn more, call the society office at 555-0148.

BRENTON, August 20 — Havenbrook Home announced today that it has selected Ashgrove Weaving Co. as the supplier for its new seasonal textiles range, which will reach all Havenbrook stores this fall.
Ashgrove Weaving Co. began as a small family workshop in Marlstead and spent its early years producing woven goods from a rented mill in Kingsford. After steady growth, the company moved its operations to a modern facility in Calverton, where it is based today.
To introduce the range, Havenbrook Home will host the Autumn Living Showcase on October 6 at its Brenton flagship store. Visitors can view the full collection and meet the design team, and admission is free.
For interviews or images, please contact the Havenbrook Home communications office.
